generation.hypothesis: A machine learning‐guided processing strategy that optimizes thermo‐mechanical parameters to create heterogeneous or gradient microstructures will overcome the conventional strength–ductility trade‐off in structural alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: Alloys with a conventional, homogeneous microstructure that exhibit a clear inverse relationship between strength and ductility.
generation.intervention: Apply data‐driven (machine learning) models to correlate processing conditions with microstructural features (e.g., gradient grain size, phase distributions, interface coherency) and then guide the fabrication via tailored thermo‐mechanical processing.
generation.conditions: Room temperature, quasi‐static deformation, and standard casting/rolling procedures with optimized processing parameters as identified by the machine learning model.
generation.structural_mediator: Tailored heterogeneous (or gradient) microstructures featuring engineered phase distributions and grain size variations.
generation.mechanism: The engineered gradient microstructures promote strain partitioning and activate additional deformation mechanisms that delay necking while preserving barriers to dislocation motion, thereby simultaneously enhancing strength and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys with machine learning–optimized gradient structures will show a measurable increase in tensile strength without compromising ductility compared to their conventionally processed homogeneous counterparts.
generation.baseline: Conventionally processed alloys that have high strength typically exhibit low ductility and vice versa, due to homogeneous microstructural characteristics.
generation.boundary: The extent of strength and ductility improvements will depend on the accuracy of the machine learning predictions and the achievable control over processing parameters; performance gains might be limited by processing heterogeneities not captured by the model.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract High-performance refractory alloys with ultrahigh strength and ductility are in demand for a wide range of critical applications, such as plasma-facing components. However, it remains challenging to increase the strength of these alloys without seriously compromising their tensile ductility. Here, we put forward a strategy to “defeat” this trade-off in tungsten refractory high-entropy alloys by stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitations (SCCPs). The coherent interfaces of SCCPs facilitate the dislocation transmission and relieve the stress concentrations that can lead to premature crack initiation. As a consequence, our alloy displays an ultrahigh strength of 2.15 GPa with a tensile ductility of 15% at ambient temperature, with a high yield strength of 1.05 GPa at 800 °C. The SCCPs design concept may afford a means to develop a wide range of ultrahigh-strength metallic materials by providing a pathway for alloy design. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Mechanical engineering

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

decision.trend: Early studies relied on conventional single‐phase strategies such as grain refinement or precipitation hardening that boosted strength at the expense of ductility. Subsequent work shifted to creating heterogeneous, multiphase, or gradient microstructures—examples being the eutectic lamellar structures or dual-phase architectures produced via stepwise thermo‐mechanical processing—which can activate strain partitioning and other mechanisms to delay necking and improve ductility while retaining high strength.
decision.unsolved: Despite promising results, the optimal design and control of heterogeneous or gradient microstructures—specifically tailoring phase distributions, grain size variations, and interface coherency—to simultaneously maximize strength and ductility remain unresolved due to the complex, multidimensional interplay of processing parameters and microstructural evolution.
decision.lever: Developing and applying machine learning models that correlate processing conditions with resulting gradient or heterogeneous microstructure parameters (e.g., phase fraction, spatial distribution, grain boundaries) to predict and optimize strength–ductility performance.
decision.why: As the trend shows a move toward complex, multi‐phase design strategies that enable concurrent improvements, a data‐driven approach can systematically explore the vast processing–structure–property space. This method can identify the optimal gradient or heterogeneous microstructures and processing routes that balance strength and ductility, addressing the current challenge of manual trial‐and‐error design.
